transcript.text: My Beko keeps stopping randomly in the middle of a wash with water still in it. Sometimes it's fine for a week, then it does it twice in a day. The model starts WTG I think. I've cleaned the filter. Driving me mad.

Intermittent faults are the most annoying kind. The fact that it's random rather than every wash narrows things down.

## First, a few things to note next time it happens

1. Does the display show anything? A code like E01–E09, flashing lights, or a frozen time is your best clue. Beko machines often show codes even on models with simple displays (sometimes as a pattern of flashing LEDs). Write it down or take a photo.
2. Is it genuinely stuck, or just paused? Wait 10–15 minutes. Some Beko programmes pause mid-cycle to let foam settle or to rebalance a load, then carry on.
3. What stage is it at? Mid-wash, before rinse, or just before spin?
4. What was in it? A single heavy item (towels, jeans, a duvet) or a lot of detergent?

## Likely causes, roughly most to least common

1. Too much foam
If you use a lot of detergent, or non-low-suds products, the machine detects excess suds and stops or pauses with water in. This fits the "fine for a week, then twice in a day" pattern because it depends on the load and dose.
→ Try cutting detergent by a third for a week and see if it stops happening.

2. Unbalanced load
If it can't distribute the load, it may stop before spin with water still in.
→ Avoid washing single bulky items alone. Mix large and small items.

3. Partial drain blockage (beyond the filter)
Cleaning the filter is good, but debris can sit in the pump impeller behind it, or the drain hose can be kinked or pushed too far down the standpipe.
→ With the filter out, shine a torch in and gently turn the impeller with a finger. It should spin freely with a slight clunk. Check the hose behind the machine isn't squashed.

4. Worn motor carbon brushes
Many Beko motors use carbon brushes. When they wear down, the motor cuts out intermittently, often mid-wash. This is more likely if the machine is 4+ years old, or if you've noticed any burning smell or the drum not turning while the machine still seems "on."
→ The brushes are cheap and replaceable, but it means taking the back off. Only do this if you're comfortable, and unplug it first.

5. Door lock, pressure switch, or control board
These are less common but possible, especially if you're getting a specific error code.

## To get water out when it stops

Unplug it, put towels and a shallow tray down, and drain through the small emergency hose next to the filter (if your model has one) or by slowly unscrewing the filter.

If you can tell me the full model number (on a sticker inside the door rim) and any code or flashing lights you see next time, I can help narrow it down much further.

Right, so the time freezes on the display when it stops, and sometimes there's a flashing light, I think it's the start one, but I can't make out any proper code. I use a measured pod so no foam, and it happens with full and half loads. Machine's about 6 years old. I'm not taking the back off though, not comfortable with that. Cleaned the filter twice, only fluff in it.

Those details help a lot. Pods and the fact that it happens with any load size make foam and imbalance much less likely. A frozen timer with a flashing Start light usually means the machine has paused itself because something told it to stop, rather than finishing a stage normally.

## Most likely causes now

1. Worn motor carbon brushes (top suspect at 6 years old)
When brushes wear down, contact with the motor becomes patchy. The motor drops out, the machine notices the drum isn't turning, and it stops with water in. This fits "random, then twice in a day" well, because it depends on how the worn brush happens to sit.

2. Door lock playing up
If the lock briefly loses contact mid-cycle, the machine stops for safety. Door locks are a common failure on machines this age.

3. A loose electrical connection or power blip
This is less common, but it's easy to rule out.

## Things you can check without taking the back off

• Power: If it's on an extension lead or adaptor, plug it straight into the wall. Try a different socket if you can.
• Door: Make sure the door seal isn't folded over at the latch side. Look at the plastic hook on the door for cracks or wear. Shut the door firmly.
• Drain hose: Check it isn't kinked behind the machine or pushed more than about 15cm down the standpipe.

## Next time it stops, try this. It's the most useful test.

1. Listen before touching anything. Do you hear a hum or clicking as if it's trying to turn the drum?
2. Press Start once. Does it carry on? Does it run for a bit, then stop again?
3. If nothing happens, switch off at the wall for 2 minutes, then back on and press Start.

What this tells you:
• Hum or click but the drum won't turn, or it restarts then stops again soon after: this points to the motor brushes.
• It won't restart, or the door lock light flickers: this points to the door lock.

## Finding out what the flashing light means

Look for a sticker inside the door rim or on the back of the door. It will have the full model number, starting WTG. Search that number on Beko's website for the manual. Many Beko models without a code display use specific light patterns to show faults, and the manual explains them. You can also ring Beko with the model number and describe the symptoms.

## If it needs a repair

Brushes and door locks are both cheap parts, and either is a routine job for an engineer. So it's normally worth repairing a 6-year-old machine rather than replacing it, unless the motor itself or the control board turns out to be the problem. If you tell the engineer what the restart test showed, it'll save them time and you money.
